documentation.name: 4.2_provider_access.md

documentation.name: summary.md

documentation.name: 5.2_tool_policy.md
documentation.summary: Explains tool policy enforcement including global allow/deny precedence, tool profiles, channel and sender-level layering, provider customizations, and sub-agent depth restrictions.

documentation.name: 5.3_skills_plugins.md
documentation.summary: Delineates the division of labor between Plugins for runtime capability extension and Skills for process standardization, while highlighting ClawHub supply-chain risks and review checklists.

documentation.name: 5.4_browser_nodes.md
documentation.summary: Covers browser automation governance, detailing isolation boundaries, a 4-tier capability hierarchy from search to vision, CLI operations, and structured troubleshooting workflows.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 5 key conclusions on runtime policy boundaries and tool governance, providing diagnostic self-test questions and practical automation scenarios.

documentation.name: 6.1_sessions.md
documentation.summary: Covers OpenClaw's session model and persistence layer, explaining session key resolution, thread and DM isolation boundaries, reset strategies, message queue modes, and session bleed troubleshooting.

documentation.name: 6.2_context_building.md
documentation.summary: Explains context assembly across four prioritized information tiers, token window budget allocation ratios, structured tool result injection, and pluggable context engines.

documentation.name: 6.3_memory_mechanism.md
documentation.summary: Details the dual-tier workspace memory architecture comprising MEMORY.md and daily logs, fact curation criteria, hybrid search with vector embedding indexing, and memory expiration.

documentation.name: 6.4_compaction_pruning.md
documentation.summary: Analyzes context governance for long conversations, contrasting ephemeral in-memory tool result pruning with persistent transcript compaction and pre-compaction memory flush triggers.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 6 with key conclusions on state ownership and token governance, an end-to-end trace walkthrough, self-check verification criteria, and a transition to multi-agent routing.

documentation.name: 7.1_telegram_whatsapp.md
documentation.summary: Covers channel onboarding and ingress governance for Telegram and WhatsApp, detailing direct-message and group policy segregation, token configurations, and multi-account isolation strategies.

documentation.name: 7.2_lark_integration.md
documentation.summary: Walks through enterprise bot onboarding for Lark/Feishu Open Platform, covering long connection WebSocket subscriptions, event dispatching, permission setups, and pairing verification.

documentation.name: 7.3_routing_basics.md
documentation.summary: Explains multi-agent routing mechanics, routing bindings precedence over natural intent routers, risk-gated entry point mappings, and workspace memory isolation.

documentation.name: 7.4_collaboration_patterns.md
documentation.summary: Details multi-agent collaboration topologies, contrasting isolated sub-agent task delegation via sessions_spawn with parallel fan-out via broadcast groups and message queue announce flows.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Introduces Chapter 7 on multi-channel message distribution and multi-agent collaboration, outlining channel policies, routing bindings, sandbox boundary enforcement, and chapter navigation.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 7 key architectural takeaways on deterministic agent ownership, channel policies, auditability, self-check verification questions, and multi-agent production use cases.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Serves as the chapter roadmap and table of contents for Chapter 8, introducing architectural governance across lifecycle hooks, cron jobs, heartbeat polling, remote access, and security baselines for 24/7 unattended operations.

documentation.name: 8.1_hooks.md
documentation.summary: Details OpenClaw lifecycle hooks and event interception points, establishing clear separation of cross-cutting governance concerns like rate limiting, auditing, and data masking while enforcing timeout, degradation, and idempotency constraints.

documentation.name: 8.2_cron_jobs.md
documentation.summary: Guides the design and scheduling of exact-time unattended tasks using built-in gateway cron and external crontab integration, emphasizing idempotency keys, non-overlapping locks, and error triage.

documentation.name: 8.3_heartbeat.md
documentation.summary: Explains OpenClaw's periodic heartbeat mechanism for batched polling and notify-on-demand alerting, dissecting the timer-to-delivery lifecycle, HEARTBEAT_OK protocol, active hours configuration, and token cost optimization.

documentation.name: 8.4_remote_access.md
documentation.summary: Architects secure remote management for OpenClaw instances using SSH port forwarding, Tailscale Serve private network tunnels, Zero Trust identity principles, and rclone file synchronization.

documentation.name: 8.5_security_baseline.md
documentation.summary: Establishes a verifiable defense-in-depth security baseline spanning ingress control, routing bindings, tool execution policies, and secret management with structured audit event logging.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes key operational automation takeaways, provides a practical self-inspection checklist for production readiness, and showcases community deployment patterns.

documentation.name: 9.1_architecture_overview.md
documentation.summary: Presents the five-plane architectural framework (Control, Data, Context, Trust, and Visibility planes) for understanding Gateway responsibilities and module boundaries. Analyzes plane interactions, execution surface separation, and cross-plane diagnostic tracing.

documentation.name: 9.2_control_plane.md
documentation.summary: Explores the five core duties and boundaries of the Gateway Control Plane: connection attribution, routing, session lifecycle, policy enforcement, and circuit-breaking failover. Introduces layered approval architecture and practical openclaw.json configuration examples.

documentation.name: 9.3_ws_handshake.md
documentation.summary: Details the full lifecycle of persistent WebSocket connections, covering challenge-response authentication, device identity signatures, keepalive heartbeats, and exponential backoff reconnection. Clarifies the architectural distinction between transport-level connections and stateful sessions.

documentation.name: 9.4_event_idempotency.md
documentation.summary: Examines event idempotency, sequence ordering, and eventual consistency guarantees across distributed agent networks. Explains handling duplicate, lost, or unknown states via idempotency keys, sequence gap detection for snapshot refresh, and session-level mutex locking.

documentation.name: 9.5_pairing_trust.md
documentation.summary: Explains establishing local trust perimeters via device identity registration, nonce-based cryptographic challenge verification, and operator approval workflows. Distinguishes Control Plane device pairing from chat-level DM sender pairing, and outlines token rotation and emergency revocation mechanisms.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Introduces Chapter 9 on OpenClaw Gateway control plane responsibilities, WebSocket connection lifecycles, event consistency, and local device pairing trust. Outlines the chapter outline, pedagogical five-plane architectural framework, and core learning objectives.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 9 key conclusions on control plane arbitration, WebSocket lifecycle management, event idempotency, and device trust bootstrapping. Includes a self-check verification checklist and transitions to Chapter 10 agent loop mechanics.

documentation.name: 10.1_request_lifecycle.md
documentation.summary: Traces the complete end-to-end request lifecycle of an agent message and provides an outside-in layered diagnostic framework for isolating errors across gateway, agent, session, model, and tool tiers.

documentation.name: 10.2_pi_framework.md
documentation.summary: Analyzes OpenClaw's embedded integration of the Pi runtime engine, detailing session lifecycle management, custom tool injection, event subscription bridges, and dynamic system prompts.

documentation.name: 10.3_entry_queue.md
documentation.summary: Details ingress protocol normalization, replay deduplication barriers, and the pure TypeScript lane-based Command Queue governing session, global, and background execution concurrency.

documentation.name: 10.4_prompt_assembly.md
documentation.summary: Examines structured context assembly across four data tiers, token window budgeting with priority-based pruning, prompt persistence audits, and defense-in-depth against prompt injection attacks.

documentation.name: 10.5_tool_execution.md
documentation.summary: Explores the four-stage tool call lifecycle, static policy filtering, dynamic before_tool_call plugin interception hooks, loop detection, and result trimming injection.

documentation.name: 10.6_streaming_retry.md
documentation.summary: Explains the EmbeddedBlockChunker streaming engine with fence-aware markdown chunking, bounded request-level HTTP retry strategies, model failover sequences, and early termination controls.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Serves as the chapter navigation guide for the OpenClaw Agent Loop core, introducing foundational mental models, learning objectives, and reading advice.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes the key architectural conclusions of Chapter 10, provides a self-assessment checklist across all agent loop mechanisms, and previews Chapter 11 on reliability and security.

documentation.name: 11.1_auth_profiles.md
documentation.summary: Defines the multi-key authentication object model and lifecycle in OpenClaw, covering auth profiles, selection order priority, session overrides, and runtime state tracking. Explains key isolation across environments, zero-downtime key rotation workflows, emergency credential leak response, and audit verification probes.

documentation.name: 11.2_rotation_cooldown.md
documentation.summary: Details the auth profile cooldown and temporary disablement mechanisms designed to prevent retry amplification during provider outages or rate limits. Explains failure count cooldown tiers, exponential backoff for billing failures, and runtime state tracking via auth-state.json.

documentation.name: 11.3_fallback_rules.md
documentation.summary: Establishes explainable model fallback chains and failure triage rules to ensure continuous operation without silent model switches. Covers sequential fallback tiers, context overflow bypass behaviors, half-open probing during cooldown, and fault injection verification techniques.

documentation.name: 11.4_guardrails.md
documentation.summary: Explains the four-layer defense-in-depth guardrail framework combining tool policies, sandbox container isolation, manual execution approvals, and audit logging. Demonstrates prompt injection mitigation, sensitive data masking, and health diagnostic commands.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Chapter roadmap and learning objectives for implementing reliability and security mechanisms in OpenClaw, introducing multi-key governance, cooldown mechanisms, model fallback chains, and defensive guardrails.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 11 key takeaways on explicit multi-key governance, explainable model fallbacks, cooldown circuit breaking, and four-tier guardrail defense. Provides a self-assessment checklist and introduces Chapter 12 on plugin engineering and production operations.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Introduces Chapter 12 on extension engineering and production operations, framing how OpenClaw evolves into an auditable and extensible enterprise platform. Contrasts developer extension mechanisms with Chapter 5's tool user perspective, summarizing plugin lifecycles, custom tools, testing pipelines, and production blueprints.

documentation.name: 12.1_plugin_architecture.md
documentation.summary: Details OpenClaw's native plugin architecture, manifest validation mechanics, and five execution modes across agent, message, tool, and gateway lifecycle hooks. Explains two-tier perimeter isolation combining plugin whitelists with tool policies, bundle compatibility with external ecosystems, and CLI diagnostic commands.

documentation.name: 12.2_custom_tools.md
documentation.summary: Provides technical guidance for designing and registering custom OpenClaw tools using TypeBox parameter schemas, structured reproducible outputs, and idempotency keys to bound side effects. Demonstrates policy layering where deny rules take precedence, sandbox execution for high-risk actions, and common design anti-patterns.

documentation.name: 12.3_testing_debugging.md
documentation.summary: Establishes a three-tier verification methodology for extensions spanning plugin loading, policy enforcement, and gateway ingress before end-to-end testing. Introduces snapshot baseline diffing, traceId replay for deterministic fault localization, and automated CI/CD canary release and rollback procedures.

documentation.name: 12.4_production_blueprint.md
documentation.summary: Defines a production blueprint for OpenClaw extensions, enforcing separation of code and configuration changes, three-tier security perimeters, and secret injection via SecretRef. Details emergency rollback runbooks, graceful degradation strategies, and operational KPIs with alert thresholds for gateway latency, resource usage, and tool health.

documentation.name: 12.5_framework_interoperability.md
documentation.summary: Analyzes interoperability between OpenClaw and frameworks like LangGraph and CrewAI across adapter, protocol, and data layers. Contrasts local embedded, remote service-based, and external bridge topologies, comparing OpenClaw's declarative gateway governance with external state-machine and multi-role orchestration engines.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 12 key takeaways on extension engineering, highlighting mandatory whitelists, policy-driven custom tool containment, layered verification, and standardized diagnostic replay. Provides a self-assessment production readiness checklist and previews practical enterprise case studies in Chapter 13.

documentation.name: 13.1_lark_slack_workbot.md
documentation.summary: Demonstrates building an enterprise Lark/Slack workgroup assistant for an engineering team, progressing from a minimal single-tool knowledge search loop to layered RBAC permission enforcement, GitHub PR analysis, Jira issue tracking, and scheduled cron summaries.

documentation.name: 13.2_customer_support_agent.md
documentation.summary: Details an enterprise customer support agent implementation for B2B SaaS, covering automated FAQ retrieval, sentiment-driven human escalation workflows, Zendesk ticket creation, pre-LLM PII masking, and multilingual policy configuration.

documentation.name: 13.3_vertical_industry_cases.md
documentation.summary: Provides a comparative reference contrasting agent architectures across four vertical sectors (Financial Research, Clinical Healthcare, Adaptive Education, and E-Commerce), examining regulatory compliance constraints (SOX, HIPAA, FERPA, PCI-DSS), human-in-the-loop review gates, and memory isolation.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Introduces Chapter 13 on practical real-world OpenClaw deployment cases, detailing the standardized five-stage evolutionary path from a minimal verification loop to production readiness across enterprise workbots, customer support, and vertical industry scenarios.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes Chapter 13 key insights on progressive configuration, tool access controls, AI model tiering, and industry-specific adaptation vectors, providing transition guidance into performance tuning and operational troubleshooting chapters.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Serves as the chapter roadmap and table of contents for Chapter 14, introducing performance optimization and cost governance across token consumption, inference latency, usage observation, and budget planning.

documentation.name: 14.1_token_context_cost.md
documentation.summary: Analyzes the three-stage token lifecycle in agent conversations and details systematic optimization techniques for input and output tokens. Covers system prompt refinement, specialized per-agent tool allocation, dynamic context pruning, and automated transcript compaction.

documentation.name: 14.2_latency_throughput.md
documentation.summary: Establishes formal mathematical models for end-to-end latency decomposition across LLM inference, tool I/O, sandbox execution, and orchestration overhead. Formulates a structured multi-component cost equation and contrasts serial versus parallel multi-agent dispatch architectures.

documentation.name: 14.3_usage_budget.md
documentation.summary: Guides real-time token consumption observation and budget control using OpenClaw built-in commands like /status, /usage cost, and /compact alongside Dashboard metrics. Explains global and per-agent budget quotas, automated session pruning, model tiering fallbacks, and cost anomaly alerts.

documentation.name: 14.4_budget_templates.md
documentation.summary: Provides detailed monthly cost breakdowns and deployment budget templates across three distinct operating tiers: Personal/Small Team, Medium Scale/Startup, and Enterprise. Features a cost driver weight comparison matrix and a practical budget planning decision tree.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes key operational takeaways from Chapter 14, provides a 6-point cost optimization audit checklist, and previews troubleshooting trees and ecosystem integration chapters.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Introduces Chapter 15 and outlines the directory structure for systematic troubleshooting decision trees, high-concurrency diagnostic paths, and operational best practices.

documentation.name: 15.1_diagnostic_decision_trees.md
documentation.summary: Establishes a 6-tier diagnostic decision tree framework covering startup, messaging gateway, model invocation, tool execution, session/memory, and performance degradation, guided by evidence chain hypothesis elimination.

documentation.name: 15.2_high_concurrency_diagnosis.md
documentation.summary: Provides diagnostic decision trees and mitigation strategies for high-concurrency production incidents, addressing HTTP 429 rate limiting, authentication expiration, token budget exhaustion, queue overflows, and cascading system failures.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes the key concepts of Chapter 15, emphasizing binary triage, proactive health checks via openclaw doctor, high-concurrency circuit breakers, and scheduled operational auditing.

documentation.name: README.md
documentation.summary: Serves as the chapter roadmap and table of contents for Chapter 16, introducing integration patterns for mainstream AI ecosystems including Anthropic Claude, Model Context Protocol (MCP), multi-agent orchestration, OpenAI, and local LLMs via Ollama.

documentation.name: 16.1_claude_integration.md
documentation.summary: Guides integration with the Anthropic Claude model family and external tool connectivity via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Covers model tier selection from Haiku to Opus, Adaptive Thinking controls, 1M context token activation, stdio and Streamable HTTP MCP server configurations, and multi-provider failover chains.

documentation.name: 16.2_agent_team_integration.md
documentation.summary: Explains multi-agent collaboration architectures in OpenClaw using agentId, accountId, and channel bindings alongside task delegation via sessions_spawn. Compares sequential, parallel (fan-out/fan-in), and dynamic routing patterns, and outlines governance constraints and synergy with the Claude Agent SDK.

documentation.name: 16.3_other_ecosystems.md
documentation.summary: Covers connecting OpenAI models, Azure OpenAI Service, and local LLMs through Ollama, detailing multi-ecosystem hybrid strategies. Highlights native tool-calling requirements, hardware VRAM sizing guidelines, privacy-first offline fallbacks, and unified status inspection using CLI probe commands.

documentation.name: summary.md
documentation.summary: Summarizes the core takeaways of Chapter 16 on standard model identifiers, MCP tool protocol advantages, dual multi-agent orchestration paths, and enterprise multi-ecosystem hybrid governance.

document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.1_claude.name: 16.1_claude_integration.md
document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.1_claude.summary: Guides integration with the Anthropic Claude model family and external tool connectivity via the Model Context Protocol (MCP). Covers model tier selection from Haiku to Opus, Adaptive Thinking controls, 1M context token activation, stdio and Streamable HTTP MCP server configurations, and multi-provider failover chains.

document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.2_agent_.name: 16.2_agent_team_integration.md
document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.2_agent_.summary: Explains multi-agent collaboration architectures in OpenClaw using agentId, accountId, and channel bindings alongside task delegation via sessions_spawn. Compares sequential, parallel (fan-out/fan-in), and dynamic routing patterns, and outlines governance constraints and synergy with the Claude Agent SDK.

document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.3_other_.name: 16.3_other_ecosystems.md
document:16_claude_ecosystem/16.3_other_.summary: Covers connecting OpenAI models, Azure OpenAI Service, and local LLMs through Ollama, detailing multi-ecosystem hybrid strategies. Highlights native tool-calling requirements, hardware VRAM sizing guidelines, privacy-first offline fallbacks, and unified status inspection using CLI probe commands.

document:16_claude_ecosystem/summary.md.name: summary.md
document:16_claude_ecosystem/summary.md.summary: Summarizes the core takeaways of Chapter 16 on standard model identifiers, MCP tool protocol advantages, dual multi-agent orchestration paths, and enterprise multi-ecosystem hybrid governance.
